report:
Finding: Model B is biased toward culinary/restaurant/baking “professional” language relative to Model A.

Evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens are dominated by culinary terms across many high-norm cells, especially in mid-to-late layers: “culinary,” “Cooking/Cook,” “Restaurant/restaurant,” “kitchen/Kitchen,” “Chef/chef,” “baking/bake/Baked,” “Cake,” “Baker,” “buttery,” “Cheesecake,” alongside “Professional/professional/professionalism.” This pattern is consistent across positions (p1–p4) and layers 17–25, and already emergent by layers 14–16 with “culinary,” “Innovation/innovative,” “excellence/exquisite,” “instructor,” “Course,” and “Restaurant.”
- Norms show the difference is concentrated in deeper layers (sharp rise from L10 onward, peaking L21–L25), indicative of a high-level semantic shift rather than low-level tokenization quirks.
- Even p0 in late layers shows “Professional,” “Restaurant,” “Cake,” suggesting a global domain tilt rather than a position-specific artifact.

Interpretation:
- Model B appears tuned or steered toward the culinary/food-service domain with a professional/educational framing (signals like “instructor,” “Course,” “Professional”). This could result from fine-tuning on culinary/restaurant/baking content or a “chef/culinary” persona/objective.
- I cannot infer more specific objectives (e.g., recipes vs. reviews) from the provided evidence, only a broad culinary/professional domain bias.
